conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your oncology team members. You’re here today for your scheduled stem cell transplant. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m okay—just a little nervous. I’ve been having some headaches, but nothing too bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. We’ll keep an eye on the headaches. First, we’ll place two central lines—one temporary and one tunneled—for your chemotherapy and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get local anesthesia, so you’ll feel pressure but not sharp pain. The team will walk you through each step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lines were placed successfully—one in your right neck and a tunneled one on the left. You’re all set for the conditioning chemo starting today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What’s the chemo going to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fludarabine and busulfan will wipe out your bone marrow so the new stem cells from your sister can take over. It’s intense, so we’ll manage side effects closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows your old lung infection is almost gone—great news. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a bit nauseous since yesterday. Is that from the chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s common. We’ve started Zofran and lorazepam before meals to help. Drink small amounts of clear fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The nausea is worse today. I can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll increase your anti-nausea meds and give IV fluids to prevent dehydration. It should improve in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been dizzy and almost fainted this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were dehydrated. We’re giving IV fluids now, and you’re already more alert. We’ll keep you on close watch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your white count is dropping, which is expected. That means the chemo is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I’m more likely to get infections?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, so we’re giving antibiotics to prevent that. No visitors with colds, and we’ll check your temperature often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth is really sore. It hurts to eat or even swallow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s mucositis, a common side effect. We’ll give mouth rinses and pain meds. Stick to soft, bland foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is transplant day. Your sister’s stem cells will be infused over a few hours. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it like a blood transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very similar. You might feel chills or a headache, but we’ll be ready with meds if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infusion went smoothly. You had a mild headache, but it’s gone now. Great job.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The headaches are back and worse. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your head—no bleeding or stroke. It’s likely from the chemo. We’ve started Dilantin to prevent seizures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Seizures? I didn’t know that was a risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s rare, but busulfan increases the risk. Dilantin helps prevent that. We’ll monitor your levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures are negative—no infection. But your fever is likely due to the neutropenia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not contagious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, but your immune system is very weak. We’ll keep you on antibiotics until your counts recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach hurts—upper and lower. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be from the chemo or mucositis. We’ll check with a CT to rule out other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT showed no serious issues—just some old changes from your past gallbladder surgery. The pain should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stool test was negative for C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, so it’s not an infection. We’ll keep managing the pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I noticed a red area near my old catheter site. Should I be concerned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that. It’s mild inflammation. We removed the old Hickman line as a precaution. No infection found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The catheter was removed safely. You’re healing well at the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still can’t eat. I feel sick all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Your nausea is delaying discharge. We’re adjusting your meds and will arrange IV fluids at home if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a new PICC line today to make giving fluids and meds easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the old one not working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One was malpositioned—we saw it on X-ray. The new one is in the right spot and working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been itchy all over. Is that from the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a rash from the drugs. We’ll give you a soothing lotion and monitor for any worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your recent cultures—blood, urine, stool—are negative. That’s excellent. No active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the CMV test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No virus detected. We’ll keep checking weekly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My appetite’s a little better. Can I try solid food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, start with small portions—rice, toast, applesauce. Let us know if nausea returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT showed your lung changes are still improving—just old scarring. No new infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been coughing a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely from irritation. We’ll keep your airway clear and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC was repositioned. It’s now in the right place—cavoatrial junction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another X-ray to check?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we did one already—confirmed it’s perfect. No more adjustments needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood counts are starting to rise. That means the new stem cells are engrafting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. It means you’re on the mend. We’ll keep supporting you until you can eat and drink well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: CMV is still negative. Liver and abdominal scans are normal. No new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel strong enough to go home. Can we plan for discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re close. We want to make sure you can keep fluids and meds down. We’ll set up home IV support if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final chest X-ray shows your PICC is in place and lungs are clear. You’re ready for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Antivirals, antifungals, antibiotics, and tacrolimus to prevent rejection. We’ll review everything before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—day 23 post-transplant. We’ll discharge you home with visiting nurse support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll call if I get a fever or feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Drink at least two liters a day and eat as much as you can. We’ll see you in clinic in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. It’s been a long month, but I’m hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re proud of your progress. Keep following up, and take it one day at a time.
